name: Gingivectomy

lead: Gingivectomy is a dental procedure in which part of the gum is cut away. Periodontists have used it for decades to remove overgrown tissue and reduce gum pockets, and in appearance circles it is used to shorten a gummy smile so more tooth and less gum shows.

A dentist or periodontist trims a strip of gum with a scalpel, electrosurgical unit or laser and lets it heal. Where the extra gum display comes from tissue overgrowth or delayed tooth eruption, trimming exposes more of the tooth crown. Dental sources describe up to about 3 mm of gum display when smiling as commonly considered typical. Research is substantial for gum disease and healing, with fewer, smaller studies on gummy-smile cases specifically.

paras: It is done in a dental chair under local anaesthetic after a diagnosis of what causes the gum display. When the cause is the jawbone, upper lip or tooth position, other procedures are usually discussed instead. Good plaque control afterwards matters.

Reported issues include pain for a few days, bleeding, slow healing, tissue regrowth if plaque control is poor, and recession that can open dark gaps called black triangles between teeth. Electrosurgery may cause more damage to neighbouring tissue than a scalpel. It is a clinician-performed procedure.

chain: Less gum showing in a smile
angle.text: Gingivectomy reshapes gum tissue to reduce a gummy smile or remove overgrown gums so more of the tooth shows. The change is visible once it heals, and the procedure is long established in dentistry.

lead: Gingivectomy is a dental surgical procedure in which part of the gum tissue (gingiva) is removed. It is described as the oldest surgical approach in periodontal (gum disease) therapy and is usually performed either for appearance or to improve the outlook for a tooth [1][2]. Common indications include suprabony periodontal pockets, enlarged gums (including drug-induced overgrowth), exposing more tooth for restorations, and reducing excessive gum display when smiling [1][1].

In looksmaxxing, the procedure is listed among hard (surgical) interventions because it can shorten the visible gum band in a "gummy smile". Dental sources describe up to about 3 mm of gum display when smiling as commonly considered acceptable, with more than that classed as a gummy smile [2]. Whether a gum-only procedure suits a given smile depends on the cause, which can include altered passive eruption, bony or lip factors [1].

Clinical research on gingivectomy is substantial but mostly concerns periodontal disease, gingival enlargement and healing, including trials comparing scalpel and laser techniques and adjunct therapies such as low-level laser. Published studies of gummy-smile procedures specifically are fewer and smaller.

paras: In a gingivectomy the clinician excises gum tissue to reduce pocket depth, reshape the gum line or expose tooth structure. It is described as the main historical treatment for reducing pocket depth in periodontitis, particularly suprabony pockets, where removing the pocket wall gives access for removing calculus [2].

Other indications include gingival enlargement, such as drug-induced overgrowth when severe, and hereditary gingival fibromatosis, where recurrence is described as unpredictable [2]. It can also expose sound tooth structure for restorative work when decay or fracture lies below the gum line [2][3].

Dental references describe gum display of up to about 3 mm on smiling as commonly regarded as acceptable, and display beyond this as a gummy smile, which can be corrected by gingivectomy when tissue excess is the cause [2]. Conditions that need bone surgery, or where the pocket base extends beyond the mucogingival junction, are listed as contraindications, as are some aesthetic cases in the front of the upper jaw [2].

A registered trial has compared different periodontal plastic surgery techniques for gummy smile, and another compares digital with conventional guided gingivectomy for altered passive eruption [4][5].

Scalpel gingivectomy is the traditional method. Electrosurgery uses high-frequency current to cut and coagulate; compared with a scalpel it gives a drier field and less postoperative pain but may cause more damage to adjacent tissue, slower healing and a stronger inflammatory response [2].

Lasers (Nd:YAG, CO2, diode) are also used. Proposed advantages include a bloodless field, minimal pain and no need for a surgical dressing, while animal studies have found that higher laser energy can cause scarring and delayed healing [2]. A CO2 laser report from 1985 described its use for removing phenytoin-related overgrowth [6].

Healing is reported to depend heavily on plaque control; without good hygiene and follow-up, disease and tissue overgrowth are likely to return [2]. Discomfort usually subsides within a few days, and patients may find cleaning difficult at first, so professional cleanings are advised [2].

Reported undesired outcomes include gum recession leading to black triangles between teeth [2]. An experimental dog study from 1984 examined recession at sites with a narrow band of keratinized gingiva, which is why remaining attached gingiva is a consideration in case selection [7]. A survey of patient pain after different periodontal therapies has been published in the Journal of the American Dental Association [8].

Landmark 1970s trials in Journal of Clinical Periodontology compared gingivectomy with other periodontal surgical techniques, such as flap procedures, in patients with optimal and with poor plaque control, and followed healing for up to two years [9][10]. A 2016 review discussed scaling and root planing versus conservative surgery for chronic periodontitis [11]. A review on crown lengthening describes the surgical options for exposing tooth structure [3].

A 2008 split-mouth controlled pilot study in 20 patients reported improved wound healing when low-level laser irradiation was applied after gingivectomy and gingivoplasty [12]. Registered trials include comparisons of scalpel and diode laser gingivectomy in orthodontic patients with gum overgrowth, injectable platelet-rich fibrin after gingivectomy, and herbal or synthetic gels after gum surgery [13][14][15][16].

Grokipedia credits the French dentist Pierre Fauchard with an early description in 1742 and says the term was coined by H.P. Pickerill in 1912, with the procedure developing in early 20th-century dental literature as a method of pocket elimination [1]. These details come from an AI-generated reference and have not been verified against primary sources here. Wikipedia describes it simply as the oldest surgical approach in periodontal therapy [2].
